title: Post-Quantum TLS Migration: A Systematization of Hybrid Handshakes, PSKs, KeyUpdate, and Certificate Strategies
abstract:
Post-quantum migration of Transport Layer Security (TLS) is often described as replacing a classical key-exchange algorithm with a post-quantum alternative. This framing is incomplete: TLS distributes security across key establishment, authentication, resumption and pre-shared keys (PSKs), traffic-secret evolution, and the X.509/PKIX ecosystem. These functions have different security objectives, failure modes, lifecycle dependencies, and deployment constraints. This Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) develops a functional framework for analyzing post-quantum TLS migration as an architectural problem rather than a single algorithm transition.

We systematize classical, pure post-quantum, and hybrid key establishment; TLS 1.3 PSK modes and resumption; KeyUpdate; ML-KEM; ML-DSA and SLH-DSA; hybrid and composite authentication; X.509/PKIX and trust-anchor migration; HSM dependencies; interoperability; performance; deployment environments; cryptographic inventory; and crypto-agility. We classify evidence by mechanism, security objective, source of keying material, forward-secrecy behavior, quantum threat, post-compromise behavior, communication and computational cost, interoperability dependency, standardization status, deployment evidence, and migration complexity. We explicitly separate finalized standards from evolving Internet-Drafts and implementation-specific evidence.

The systematization produces four analytical conclusions. First, confidentiality migration and authentication migration are coupled operationally but distinct security programs. Second, hybrid ECDHE-ML-KEM is a strong transitional architecture for confidentiality migration when the relevant TLS integration and implementation support are available, because its security objective can tolerate failure of one component; the exact security claim nevertheless depends on the standardized construction and its assumptions. Third, PSKs, resumption, and KeyUpdate are not interchangeable forms of rekeying: their security depends on the provenance and role of the secret, while KeyUpdate remains within an existing traffic-secret lineage and does not create an independent post-quantum secret. Fourth, deployment readiness is constrained as much by certificates, trust stores, HSMs, middleboxes, inventory, and interoperability as by primitive availability. We therefore derive a migration decision framework that prioritizes HNDL-sensitive data, controlled hybrid deployment, interoperability testing, staged authentication and PKI migration, and observable retirement of classical-only mechanisms.

     source of keying material, forward-secrecy behavior, quantum threat, post-compromise
     behavior, communication and computational cost, interoperability dependency, stan-
     dardization status, deployment evidence, and migration complexity. We explicitly
     separate finalized standards from evolving Internet-Drafts and implementation-specific
     evidence.

     port are available, because its security objective can tolerate failure of one component;
     the exact security claim nevertheless depends on the standardized construction and

2                                                           Post-Quantum TLS Migration


1    Introduction
Transport Layer Security is a principal mechanism through which Internet applications
obtain authenticated, confidential, and integrity-protected communication. TLS separates
the establishment of security parameters from the subsequent protection of application
records: the handshake negotiates parameters, authenticates communicating parties,
and establishes shared keying material, while the record layer uses derived traffic keys
to protect application data [Res26]. Quantum computing challenges this architecture
because widely deployed public- key mechanisms rely on mathematical problems that
are vulnerable to sufficiently capable quantum algorithms. The migration problem is
relevant before such a computer exists at cryptographically relevant scale. An adversary
can record encrypted traffic today and attempt to decrypt it later after obtaining the
computational capability required to attack the public-key mechanism used during the
original handshake. This harvest-now- decrypt-later (HNDL) threat makes migration
dependent on the confidentiality lifetime of information rather than solely on the date at
which quantum computing becomes capable of breaking deployed cryptography [Nat26].
The natural response might appear to be replacing classical key exchange with a post-
quantum algorithm. That view is incomplete because TLS uses asymmetric cryptography
for multiple logically distinct functions. Key establishment creates shared secret material
for the session. Authentication establishes the identity of a peer through signatures and
certificates or through another authentication mechanism. Session resumption derives
new connections from earlier security state. KeyUpdate evolves traffic secrets after the
handshake. X.509 and PKIX determine how authentication keys are encoded, certified,
distributed, and validated. A post-quantum mechanism addressing one of these functions
does not automatically secure the others. This separation is particularly important for
TLS 1.3 PSKs and KeyUpdate. PSKs can authenticate endpoints and, depending on
the selected mode, participate directly in key establishment. Their security consequently
depends on how they were generated, provisioned, protected, and related to previous
sessions. A resumption PSK derived from a classical-only connection does not retroactively
make that connection quantum- resistant. Similarly, KeyUpdate derives new traffic secrets
from an existing traffic-secret lineage. It does not perform a new ECDHE or KEM exchange
and therefore does not transform a quantum-vulnerable initial handshake into a post-
quantum one [Res26]. The post-quantum TLS literature has developed rapidly. Alnahawi
et al. provided a broad survey of post-quantum TLS in 2024, including classification and
performance evaluation [AMOW24]. Since then, NIST finalized FIPS 203, FIPS 204, and
FIPS 205, standardizing ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA [Nat24b, Nat24a, Nat24c]. IETF
work has progressed from the hybrid design draft to RFC 9954 for the general hybrid
construction [SFG26], while standalone ML-KEM key agreement and ML-DSA authentication
remain covered by evolving IETF documents [Con26, HSW26]; ECDHE-ML-KEM hybrid key
agreement is now specified by RFC 10024 [KKWS26]. These developments create a need
for a systematization that focuses not only on candidate algorithms but also on how the
individual TLS functions interact during migration. This paper makes six contributions:
1. a functional taxonomy separating key establishment, authentication, resumption and
PSKs, traffic-key evolution, PKI, deployment, and cryptographic agility; 2. a comparison
of classical, hybrid, and pure-PQ key establishment by security as-sumptions, forward
secrecy, interoperability, maturity, and communication cost;
    3. a focused analysis of PSKs and KeyUpdate that distinguishes authentication, key
establishment, and traffic-key evolution; 4. a separate treatment of PQ authentication and
X.509/PKIX migration, including signatures, certificate chains, trust anchors, HSMs, and
client compatibility; 5. a deployment-oriented synthesis of performance and interoperability
evidence; and 6. a migration framework prioritizing inventory, HNDL-sensitive information,
hybrid key establishment, interoperability, staged authentication migration, and crypto-
agility. The paper does not propose a new cryptographic protocol, primitive, combiner, or
Hridoy Roy                                                                                 3


formally validated migration algorithm; its contribution is an analytical systematization of
existing standards, research, implementation evidence, and migration guidance.


2     Background and Threat Model
2.1    TLS 1.3 and the Migration Boundary
TLS 1.3 establishes authenticated cryptographic state and then protects application
traffic using symmetric traffic keys [Res26]. For post-quantum migration, an important
architectural property is that symmetric record protection is conceptually separated from
asymmetric key establishment and authentication. Consequently, a deployment can change
the mechanism used to establish session secrets without necessarily replacing the symmetric
AEAD used to protect application records. The classical TLS 1.3 model commonly uses
ephemeral Diffie-Hellman mechanisms such as X25519. Ephemeral exchange
    provides classical forward secrecy: compromise of a long-term authentication key does
not by itself reveal previously established session keys. Quantum computation nevertheless
threatens the underlying discrete-logarithm problem, so classical forward secrecy does not
imply quantum resistance. A KEM provides a different interface. One party generates a
public/secret key pair; another party encapsulates a shared secret to the public key; and the
recipient decap- sulates the ciphertext to recover the secret. NIST FIPS 203 standardizes
ML-KEM-512, ML- KEM-768, and ML-KEM-1024 [Nat24b]. ML-KEM is therefore directly
relevant to TLS key establishment, whereas ML-DSA and SLH-DSA address signature-based
authentication and infrastructure [Nat24a, Nat24c].

2.2    Authentication and Key Establishment
TLS authentication and key establishment should be treated as separate security dimensions.
A deployment may combine classical authentication with classical key establishment,
classical authentication with hybrid key establishment, post- quantum authentication
with hybrid key establishment, post-quantum authentication with pure post-quantum key
establishment, or PSK authentication with either classical, hybrid, or post-quantum key
establishment. Replacing ECDHE with ML-KEM can protect the confidentiality of newly
established sessions against the quantum failure of classical key exchange, but it does not
make a classical certificate signature quantum-resistant. Conversely, replacing certificate
signatures does not protect historical ciphertext whose session keys were established using a
quantum- vulnerable mechanism. This distinction is the foundation of the systematization:
“PQC TLS” should not be treated as one security property. The security of a deployment is
determined by the combination of mechanisms used for key establishment, authentication,
resumption, traffic-key evolution, and PKI.

2.3    PSKs
TLS 1.3 supports PSKs obtained from session resumption and PSKs provisioned exter-
nally. RFC 9258 specifies mechanisms for importing external PSKs while binding them
to a protocol, KDF, hash function, and optional context [BW22]. Two TLS 1.3 PSK
key-exchange modes are particularly relevant. In psk_ke, the PSK is used without an ad-
ditional ephemeral key exchange. In psk_dhe_ke, the PSK is combined with an ephemeral
Diffie-Hellman exchange [Res26]. The latter demonstrates why PSK authentication and
key establishment must not be conflated: a PSK can authenticate an endpoint while fresh
ephemeral key material supplies forward-secret session entropy. For post-quantum migra-
tion, analogous configurations include PSK-only establishment, PSK plus classical ECDHE,
PSK plus a PQ KEM, and PSK plus a hybrid ECDHE/PQ KEM. These configurations
have different security properties and should be classified separately.
4                                                           Post-Quantum TLS Migration


2.4    KeyUpdate
TLS 1.3 KeyUpdate changes application traffic keys after the handshake. The new appli-
cation traffic secret is derived from the previous traffic secret using the TLS key schedule
and the “traffic upd” label [Res26]. KeyUpdate is therefore a symmetric key- evolution
mechanism rather than a new asymmetric exchange. This distinction has direct con-
sequences for post-quantum security. The resulting secrets remain downstream of S0 .
KeyUpdate does not introduce an independent KEM secret. If a future quantum attacker
can recover the original quantum- vulnerable handshake secret and obtain the required
transcript information, KeyUpdate does not provide the independent post-quantum foun-
dation required to repair that hand- shake. KeyUpdate can nevertheless provide useful
post-compromise properties. If an old traffic secret is deleted before an endpoint is later
compromised, the attacker may be unable to reconstruct that earlier generation from
a later traffic secret, assuming the one-wayness of the KDF and correct secret deletion
[Res26]. This is key evolution and limited post-compromise protection, not quantum-
resistant re-establishment.

2.5    Threat Model
The systematization considers four primary threat classes. Passive HNDL attackers record
encrypted handshakes and application traffic and retain them for future cryptanalysis. If
a captured session uses quantum-vulnerable ECDHE, future quantum computation may
enable recovery of the session secret from the public handshake transcript. Future quantum
attackers are modeled as adversaries capable of attacking classical public-key assumptions
and potentially attempting attacks against post-quantum as- sumptions. PQC should not
be interpreted as “quantum-proof”; rather, the relevant constructions are designed around
assumptions believed to resist currently known quantum algorithms. Active attackers
can modify handshake messages, attempt downgrade attacks, exploit implementation
differences, or induce fallback to weaker mechanisms. Migration introduces additional
negotiation states, making downgrade policy and transcript binding important. Endpoint
compromise is distinct from cryptographic compromise. A fully compromised endpoint
can expose current traffic secrets regardless of the algorithm used. KeyUpdate can reduce
exposure under certain temporary-compromise models, but it cannot protect an endpoint
under persistent active control. The threat model therefore separates two migration tracks:
Confidentiality migration: protect new session-key establishment against future quantum
attacks. Authentication migration: replace or augment quantum-vulnerable signatures
and PKI infrastructure.


3     SoK Methodology
3.1    Research Questions
The systematization addresses eight research questions: 1. What are the principal quantum
threats to TLS confidentiality and authentication? 2. How have standards bodies and
researchers proposed migrating TLS key establishment to PQC? 3. How do hybrid TLS
handshakes compare with classical TLS and pure-PQ approaches? 4. What roles do TLS
1.3 PSKs and KeyUpdate play in post-quantum migration? 5. What challenges arise
Hridoy Roy                                                                                  5


in post-quantum authentication and certificate migration? 6. What performance and
interoperability costs are reported? 7. Which migration strategies are appropriate for
different deployment environments?
    8. What research and deployment gaps remain?


3.2    Source Selection
The literature search was structured around authoritative standards and primary technical
literature. Sources considered include NIST standards and guidance, IETF RFCs, active
IETF Internet-Drafts, IACR and cryptographic research, peer-reviewed security and
networking research, official PKI specifications, implementation documentation containing
deployment evidence, and government cybersecurity guidance. Search terms included
combinations of “post-quantum TLS,” “TLS 1.3 ML-KEM,” “hybrid TLS,” “X25519 ML-KEM,”
“ECDHE MLKEM,” “KEM TLS,” “TLS PSK post quantum,” “TLS KeyUpdate quantum,”
“ML-DSA TLS,” “SLH-DSA TLS,” “post-quantum certificates,” “X.509 post quantum,” “PKIX
ML-DSA,” “TLS performance PQC,” “TLS interoperability PQC,” “harvest now decrypt
later,” and “crypto agility post quantum.” The search emphasizes material available
through August 15, 2026. Because IETF Internet-Drafts are works in progress, their status
is treated separately from finalized RFCs. No numerical corpus size is claimed because the
underlying manuscript does not provide a verified statistically exhaustive corpus.


3.3    Inclusion and Exclusion
A source was included when it materially addressed TLS 1.3, PQC key establishment,
hybrid key exchange, PQ authentication, TLS PSKs, KeyUpdate, X.509/PKIX migration,
TLS performance, interoperability, cryptographic migration, or deployment implications.
Primary standards and primary technical research were prioritized. The principal evidence
base excludes promotional material lacking technical evidence, generic quantum- computing
literature without TLS relevance, duplicate versions where a final publication was available,
unsupported technical claims, obsolete drafts when materially newer versions existed, and
benchmark results whose experimental conditions could not be established.


3.4    Classification Dimensions
Each approach was classified according to key-establishment mechanism, authentication
mechanism, hybridization, source of entropy, forward secrecy, quantum threat addressed,
bandwidth and computational impact, interoperability dependencies, standardization
status, deployment evidence, and migration complexity. The evidence was interpreted
qualitatively rather than converted into unexplained numerical scores.


3.5    Methodological Limitations
The field changes faster than conventional publication cycles, and Internet-Drafts may
change substantially before standardization. Performance studies also use different CPUs,
libraries, operating systems, network conditions, protocol configurations, and security
parameters. Direct numerical comparisons are therefore often inappropriate. There is also
publication bias toward successful implementations and research prototypes. Failed inter-
operability tests and unsuccessful migrations are less visible in the literature. Accordingly,
implementation availability is not treated as proof of universal deployment maturity.

3.6     Evidence Type and Status

The evidence extraction process records not only what a source says but what kind
of authority the source represents. Each extracted item is assigned an evidence type:
finalized NIST standard, Standards Track RFC, Informational RFC, active Internet-Draft,
peer-reviewed
    research, experimental implementation report, deployment report, or research proposal.
A separate status field records whether the mechanism is standardized at the algorithm
layer, standardized at the TLS integration layer, standardized at the certificate/PKIX
layer, implemented, experimentally interoperable, or deployed. This distinction prevents
a common category error: treating a finalized primitive as though its complete protocol
and deployment ecosystem were also finalized. For example, ML-KEM is a finalized NIST
standard, while particular TLS integrations remain separate protocol documents. Likewise,
ML-DSA is standardized by NIST and has standardized X.509 algorithm identifiers, while
TLS signature negotiation and broad verifier deployment involve additional specifications
and ecosystem support.




3.7     Reproducibility Protocol

The systematization is reproducible at the level of source categories, search terminology,
classification dimensions, and evidence interpretation. A future update can repeat the
search using the same topic clusters, retrieve newer standards and drafts, and reclassify
individual mechanisms without changing the analytical framework. The extraction schema
used in this revision is summarized in Table 1. No numerical “maturity score” is assigned
because the underlying evidence does not support a defensible universal scalar score. The
framework instead preserves the dimensions that determine why one mechanism may be
mature in one environment and immature in another.

4     Comparison with Existing Surveys and Systematiza-
      tions
4.1    Why Functional Decomposition Changes the Analysis
The functional decomposition exposes two recurrent category errors. The first is to equate
“post-quantum key exchange” with “post-quantum TLS.” Key establishment is only one
input to the TLS security state. The second is to treat every subsequent key change as
an independent security reset. KeyUpdate does not have that property, and resumption
can intentionally preserve a relationship to earlier connection state. The framework also
changes how migration sequencing is evaluated. If a deployment has high HNDL exposure
but a highly heterogeneous client population, the immediate priority is not necessarily PQ
authentication. Conversely, a managed enterprise with centrally controlled trust stores
may be able to experiment with PQ authentication earlier than a public-web service. The
relevant decision variables are therefore not just algorithm availability but data lifetime,
endpoint control, verifier availability, protocol support, and operational cost.

4.2    Evidence Hierarchy
Evidence is interpreted using an explicit hierarchy: 1. Finalized standards establish nor-
mative protocol or algorithm definitions. 2. Informational RFCs provide IETF-reviewed
constructions or guidance but do not have Standards Track status. 3. Active Internet-
Drafts describe evolving work and must be treated as work in progress. 4. Peer-reviewed
experiments provide empirical evidence under stated conditions. 5. Implementation
documentation establishes technical availability but not universal interoperability. 6. De-
ployment reports and operational guidance provide context about adoption and constraints.
7. Research proposals and preprints can identify emerging mechanisms but require ad-
ditional caution when used to support deployment claims. This hierarchy is especially
important in a field where the algorithm standardization cycle and the protocol-integration
cycle are not synchronized.


5     Taxonomy of Post-Quantum TLS Migration
The literature can be organized into nine migration strategies; Table 2 summarizes the
resulting strategy taxonomy.

5.1    Classical TLS
Classical TLS uses mechanisms such as X25519 or other ECDHE groups for key es-
tablishment and classical signature mechanisms for authentication. Its advantages are
mature interoperability, extensive implementation support, and predictable performance.
Its limitation is quantum vulnerability of the public-key components. Classical TLS
therefore represents the baseline from which migration proceeds rather than a long-term
quantum-resistant architecture.

5.2    Pure Post-Quantum Key Establishment
Pure PQ key establishment replaces the classical public-key exchange with a PQ mechanism
such as ML-KEM. Its primary advantage is a direct quantum-resistant key-establishment
architecture. Its principal migration risk is reliance on the PQ assumption without
the redundancy of a classical component and the need for all relevant endpoints to
support the mechanism. The current IETF ML-KEM TLS Internet-Draft defines ML-KEM-512,

5.3        Hybrid Key Establishment
Hybrid key establishment combines a classical exchange with a PQ KEM. X25519MLKEM768
is a representative construction [KKWS26]. Its transitional rationale is that the final
keying material incorporates both components, so security can remain dependent on the
surviving component if one component is compromised. Hybridization therefore addresses
two forms of uncertainty: the known long-term quantum vulnerability of classical public-
key cryptography and the residual cryptanalytic uncertainty associated with newer PQ
algorithms. The exact
    combiner and transcript integration must follow the protocol specification. Simply
concatenating two secrets is not, by itself, a complete hybrid construction.


5.4        PSK-Based Approaches
PSKs can provide authentication and, depending on the mode, contribute directly to
key establishment. Their value is greatest in environments with controlled provisioning,
such as private APIs, enterprise networks, managed infrastructure, and pre-provisioned
devices. PSK- only establishment does not automatically provide the same forward-secrecy
properties as fresh ephemeral exchange. PSK plus ephemeral exchange can retain fresh
session entropy, while PSK plus PQ or hybrid key establishment can combine controlled
authentication with quantum-resistant confidentiality. The appropriate classification
question is therefore not “PSK or PQC?” but: How was the PSK generated? How
was it provisioned and protected? What role does it play in the TLS key schedule?
Does it originate from a quantum-resistant connection? Is independent ephemeral key
establishment performed?


5.5        Post-Quantum Authentication
Post-quantum authentication replaces or augments classical signature mechanisms. ML-
DSA is the principal standardized lattice-based signature mechanism considered here,
Hridoy Roy                                                                                 9


while SLH-DSA provides a hash-based alternative [Nat24a, Nat24c]. PQ authentication
protects identity and certificate-related operations, but it does not automatically protect
the confidentiality of sessions whose keys were established using a classical mechanism.


5.6    Hybrid Authentication
Hybrid authentication combines classical and PQ signatures. Its transition rationale is
analogous to hybrid KEMs: security can be sought if at least one signature system remains
secure. The engineering challenge is greater than for a hybrid handshake because certificates
must be encoded, signed, validated, chained, stored, distributed, and understood by relying
parties. Hybrid signatures therefore require coordination across TLS implementations,
certificate authorities, HSMs, operating systems, browsers, trust stores, and certificate-
management systems.


5.7    PKI and Certificate Migration
Post-quantum certificate migration affects end-entity certificates, intermediate CAs, roots,
trust stores, issuance systems, validation software, certificate transparency infrastructure,
HSMs, and client compatibility. A deployment can migrate at several levels: PQ leaves
under classical intermediates, PQ chains, hybrid or composite certificates, or parallel
classical and PQ chains. These alternatives have different compatibility and security
properties and should not be treated as equivalent.


5.8    Crypto-Agile Migration
Crypto-agility is an architectural property rather than a cryptographic algorithm. A crypto-
agile system can replace cryptographic mechanisms without redesigning the surrounding
    application. For PQ migration, crypto-agility includes algorithm negotiation, crypto-
graphic inven- tory, modular TLS libraries, certificate lifecycle automation, configurable
trust stores, support for multiple certificate representations, algorithm policy controls,
interoperability test matrices, telemetry, and controlled rollback.


6     Hybrid Key Establishment, PSK, KeyUpdate, and
      Long-Lived Sessions
6.1    Hybrid ECDHE-ML-KEM
The principal transitional hybrid architecture combines ephemeral ECDHE with ML-KEM. In
a representative X25519MLKEM768 configuration, X25519 supplies the classical component
and ML-KEM-768 supplies the PQ component [KKWS26]. Let ZC denote the classical shared
secret and ZQ the PQ shared secret. A hybrid construction produces a value ZH that is
incorporated into the TLS key schedule. The security objective is that compromise of one
component alone should not reveal the final session secret if the other component remains
secure. The classical component retains a mature implementation ecosystem and classical
forward secrecy. The PQ component contributes resistance to future attacks against the
classical exchange. The hybrid design therefore provides a transitional architecture rather
than simply two independent exchanges executed side by side.

                                 ZH = Combine(ZC , ZQ ).                                 (3)

6.2    Forward Secrecy
Forward secrecy and quantum resistance are related but distinct. Classical ephemeral
ECDHE provides forward secrecy against compromise of long-term authentication keys
under the classical threat model. It does not protect a recorded session against a future
quantum attacker capable of solving the underlying discrete-logarithm problem. Hybrid
ECDHE-ML-KEM can combine the classical ephemeral property with a PQ component. The
precise forward-secrecy claim depends on ephemeral generation, secret deletion, KEM
security, transcript binding, and implementation correctness.


6.3    Downgrade Resistance
Migration creates multiple supported groups. A client may offer classical X25519, hybrid
X25519MLKEM768, standalone ML-KEM, or other supported groups. An active attacker may
attempt to force a connection toward a classical-only mechanism. A secure deployment
therefore needs explicit policy defining whether PQ is mandatory, preferred, or optional;
whether classical fallback is allowed; and how fallback is logged and monitored. Negotiated
security parameters must remain protected by TLS transcript authentication.


6.4    PSK Authentication Versus PSK Key Establishment
A PSK can serve as an authentication credential without being the sole source of session
entropy. This distinction is essential in migration analysis. PSK-only establishment can
be efficient, particularly in controlled systems, but its security depends strongly on the
PSK. If a
    PSK is reused, weakly generated, improperly stored, or compromised, the authentication
and key-establishment consequences can be substantial. PSK plus ephemeral exchange
introduces fresh session key material. In a PQ migration, the ephemeral exchange can be
a PQ KEM or a hybrid ECDHE-ML-KEM construction.


6.5    Resumption PSKs
TLS 1.3 resumption PSKs derive from an earlier connection. Their security must therefore
be evaluated according to the properties of the connection that produced them. If the
original connection was classical-only, the resulting resumption PSK should not be treated
as evidence that the original connection was quantum-resistant. A migration policy should
record the provenance of resumption credentials and determine whether they may be
used to establish sessions subject to a PQ security requirement. This creates a practical
migration question that is often overlooked: session resumption can preserve deployment
behavior from an earlier cryptographic generation. Migrating the


6.6    External PSKs
External PSKs are particularly useful in managed environments because organizations
can control provisioning and lifecycle operations [BW22]. Security management should
include generation, secure provisioning, storage, rotation, revocation, uniqueness, algorithm
binding, endpoint compromise, and prevention of cross-protocol reuse. The critical property
is provenance. A PSK is not post-quantum merely because it is symmetric. Its role in the
TLS key schedule and the mechanism from which its entropy originated determine the
relevant security properties.

6.7     KeyUpdate
KeyUpdate derives a new traffic secret from an existing one. It can reduce the volume
of traffic encrypted under a single traffic key and can provide useful security properties
following some endpoint compromises when old secrets are securely deleted [Res26]. It
does not perform ML- KEM. It does not perform ECDHE. It does not introduce a new
independent public-key secret. It does not repair a vulnerable certificate. It does not repair
a vulnerable initial handshake. Therefore, KeyUpdate is a traffic-key lifecycle mechanism,
not a PQ migration mecha- nism. A fresh PQ KEM exchange has a different security role
because it introduces new keying material through a new encapsulation/decapsulation oper-
ation. KeyUpdate and fresh PQ rekeying should consequently be viewed as complementary
mechanisms rather than substitutes.

6.8     Fresh PQ Rekeying
Fresh PQ rekeying is analytically distinct from KeyUpdate because it introduces new PQ-
derived keying material through a new KEM exchange. Its security value therefore depends
on the exact protocol construction, the freshness and deletion of the relevant secrets, and
the absence of an attacker-controlled endpoint. It should be evaluated as an additional
security boundary for long-lived sessions, not as a more expensive form of KeyUpdate.
The appropriate trigger is deployment-specific. Relevant variables include confidentiality
lifetime, HNDL exposure, connection duration, endpoint capability, protocol support, and
the cost of another public-key exchange. The evidence reviewed here does not justify a
universal byte, time, or message-count threshold.

A connection may involve an initial hybrid handshake, multiple KeyUpdates, resumption

security. For long-lived connections with stringent confidentiality requirements, migration
policy should define when a fresh PQ key establishment is required rather than relying
indefinitely on
    symmetric KeyUpdate. The appropriate threshold depends on the threat model, data
lifetime, protocol support, and operational cost.

The most useful way to distinguish PSKs, KeyUpdate, resumption, and fresh PQ estab-

therefore can establish a new security foundation. Table 4 summarizes these security-state

6.11       Classical Handshake Followed by KeyUpdate
Let the application traffic secret produced by the initial handshake be S0 . TLS 1.3
derives subsequent traffic secrets as Si+1 = g(Si ). If S0 ultimately depends on a quantum-
vulnerable ECDHE exchange, KeyUpdate does not introduce an independent post-quantum
secret. Therefore a future attacker capable of recovering the original classical handshake
secret does not encounter a new PQ boundary merely because the endpoint performed one
or more KeyUpdates. This does not make KeyUpdate useless. If prior traffic secrets are
correctly erased, compromise of a later traffic secret need not expose earlier generations.
That property is valuable under appropriate temporary-compromise models. It is, however,
a property of symmetric key evolution rather than post-quantum re-establishment.

6.12       Resumption as a Security-Lineage Problem
TLS 1.3 resumption credentials are derived from earlier handshake state. Consequently,
a migration policy should track the provenance of resumption credentials rather than
classifying every PSK as either “secure” or “insecure.” A resumption PSK produced by a
hybrid handshake
    is not equivalent, in provenance, to one produced by a classical-only handshake. More-
over, a resumed handshake can combine the PSK with a fresh asymmetric exchange,
changing the security properties of the new connection. The practical implication is that
Hridoy Roy                                                                                13


cryptographic inventories should record not only the existence of PSK support but also
the generation path, expiration policy, ticket lifetime, and whether resumed sessions are
required to perform a fresh PQ-capable exchange.


6.13    Post-Compromise Scenarios
The analysis distinguishes four compromise points: compromise of a long-term authentica-
tion key, compromise of a current traffic secret, compromise of a resumption credential,
and persistent endpoint compromise. These are not interchangeable. KeyUpdate is rele-
vant primarily to the traffic-secret lineage; certificate migration is relevant to long-term
authentication; resumption policy controls the lifetime of inherited connection state; and
no protocol-level rekeying mechanism can protect an endpoint that remains under persis-
tent attacker control. The unresolved policy problem is therefore not “how often should
TLS KeyUpdate run?” but “under what conditions should a deployment require a fresh
PQ-capable key establishment?” The answer depends on confidentiality lifetime, threat
model, protocol support, endpoint capability, connection duration, and operational cost.
The literature does not justify a universal time or byte threshold.


7      Post-Quantum Authentication and PKI
7.1    ML-DSA and SLH-DSA
NIST FIPS 204 standardizes ML-DSA as a lattice-based post-quantum signature mechanism
[Nat24a]. FIPS 205 standardizes SLH-DSA as a stateless hash-based alternative [Nat24c].
The two algorithms provide different cryptographic assumptions and operational trade- offs.
ML- DSA is directly relevant to TLS authentication and certificate infrastructure. SLH-DSA
provides diversification through hash-based assumptions but can involve larger signatures
and different signing and verification costs; RFC 9909 specifies SLH-DSA algorithm
identifiers for X.509/PKIX. The important migration distinction is that these algorithms
address authentication. They do not replace ML-KEM’s role in session-key establishment.


7.2    CertificateVerify and TLS Authentication
TLS authentication uses signatures to authenticate handshake state and, in certificate-
based deployments, uses certificates to bind identities to public keys [Res26]. A post-
quantum authentication deployment therefore needs compatible signature schemes for
CertificateVerify and certificate-related operations. The IETF TLS working group has
developed work describing the use of ML-DSA in TLS 1.3 [HSW26]. As of 15 August
2026, the document was at draft-ietf-tls-mldsa-05 and had been approved for publication
as an Informational RFC, but publication was being held following an appeal and it
had not yet been published as an RFC. Such work illustrates the difference between
an algorithm becoming a NIST standard and the broader protocol ecosystem becoming
deployment-ready.


7.3    X.509 and PKIX
RFC 5280 defines the Internet X.509 PKI profile and certification-path validation model
[C+ 08]. PQ certificate migration consequently involves more than adding a signature
algorithm. The infrastructure must support PQ public-key encoding, signature represen-
tation, certificate policies, signature-scheme negotiation, certificate issuance, validation,
trust-store updates, and mixed classical/PQ chains. A certificate chain may include an
end-entity certificate, intermediates, and a trust anchor. Migration can occur at each level,

7.4        CA and Trust-Anchor Migration
CA migration is slower than server-key migration because CA certificates often have long
validity periods and are distributed through browsers, operating systems, applications,
embedded devices, and enterprise trust stores. The central operational problem is verifier
availability. A CA may be able to generate a PQ certificate before browsers, operating
systems, HSMs, and application libraries can validate it. Standardizing a signature
algorithm therefore does not establish universal deployment compatibility. Trust anchors are
particularly difficult because they are frequently installed outside ordinary certificate-update
mechanisms. Migration requires overlapping validity periods, distribution mechanisms,
rollback plans, client testing, embedded trust-store updates, and controlled retirement of
classical trust anchors.


7.5        Hybrid and Composite Certificates
Hybrid or composite certificates can provide transitional compatibility by combining
classical and PQ signatures. However, certificate hybridization is operationally complex.
The certificate must be encoded, signed, validated, chained, distributed, and interpreted
consistently by all relevant parties. IETF work on composite ML-DSA signatures addresses
some of these questions for X.509/PKIX applications. Such mechanisms should remain
classified according to their actual standardization status rather than being described as
finalized Internet standards.


7.6        HSMs
Enterprise CA keys are frequently protected by HSMs. PQ migration therefore requires
HSM support for key generation, secure storage, signing, backup, recovery, certificate
issuance, rotation, and audit. This creates a recurring migration asymmetry: a cryp-
tographic algorithm can be standardized before the operational hardware required to
deploy it at scale is mature. HSM readiness should consequently be treated as a first-class
migration dependency rather than as an implementation detail.

8     Performance, Interoperability, and Deployment
8.1    Interpreting Performance Evidence
Performance results depend on CPU architecture, cryptographic library, compiler, hardware
acceleration, operating system, TLS implementation, security parameter, network RTT,
packet loss, congestion, transport protocol, certificate-chain length, resumption rate, and
concurrent connection count. Consequently, a primitive microbenchmark and an end-
to-end TLS benchmark answer different questions. A KEM may consume modest CPU
time while its larger messages increase network latency. Conversely, a network with
abundant bandwidth and low RTT may make message expansion less significant. The
literature should therefore be interpreted by measurement layer rather than by selecting
one benchmark number as universally representative.


8.2    Key and Handshake Size
FIPS 203 specifies a 1,184-byte public key and a 1,088-byte ciphertext for ML-KEM-768
[Nat24b]. These values make communication overhead an important migration considera-
tion.
    The impact is environment-dependent. Large key shares are more consequential on
mobile, satellite, IoT, embedded, and high-latency networks than on high-bandwidth local
networks.


8.3    Computational Cost
The rustls performance study reported measurable CPU cost for X25519MLKEM768 while
emphasizing that the primary benchmark did not include all networking consequences of
larger messages [rus24]. CoNEXT 2023 research similarly examined post-quantum TLS 1.3
performance under specific experimental conditions [SWH+ 23]. More recent work evaluates
classical, hybrid, and pure-PQ configurations using controlled performance frameworks
[M+ 26]. These results support an analytical conclusion rather than a universal numerical
claim: PQ TLS can introduce both computational and communication costs, and the
relative importance of each depends on the deployment environment.


8.4    Certificate Size and Latency
Certificate chains may become a major source of PQ handshake expansion. A server
can transmit an end-entity certificate, intermediate certificates, extensions, CertificateV-
erify, and other handshake data. Consequently, even if an individual PQ signature is
computationally manageable, the complete handshake can become significantly larger.
Larger messages can lead to additional packets, fragmentation, memory consumption,
congestion, and latency. Recent research specifically considers the network impact of PQ
certificate-chain sizes [CC26].

8.5     Interoperability
Interoperability requires more than algorithm-level compatibility. A complete test matrix
should include client and server libraries, operating systems, browsers, certificate types,
supported groups, signature algorithms, resumption, 0-RTT, HelloRetryRequest, proxies,
and middleboxes. Historical experimental Kyber identifiers should not automatically be
treated as equiv- alent to current ML-KEM identifiers. Implementations must agree on exact
named groups, wire formats, combiners, and protocol behavior.

8.6     Middleboxes and Large Messages
Middleboxes may react differently to unfamiliar extensions or larger handshake messages.
Migration must therefore test the complete communication path rather than only direct
client- server connections. A system that successfully negotiates hybrid TLS in a laboratory
may still fail when deployed through a proxy, load balancer, inspection device, or legacy
network component.

8.7     Constrained Devices
Embedded systems add memory, power, firmware-lifecycle, and update constraints. Their
migration cost may be dominated by the difficulty of deploying software updates rather
than by raw cryptographic CPU cost. For constrained devices, the optimization objective
is therefore better represented as a combination of security, bandwidth, memory, energy,
implementation size, and lifecycle constraints rather than CPU time alone.

8.8     Cloud and Enterprise Infrastructure
Table 6 summarizes the principal performance evidence. Cloud environments benefit from
centralized software updates but also contain large numbers of TLS termination points,
load balancers, service meshes, proxies, and internal service-to-service connections. A cloud
deployment can migrate Internet-facing TLS while leaving internal connections classical.
Enterprise PKI introduces additional dependencies: internal CAs, HSMs, automated
issuance, legacy applications, device certificates, VPNs, smart cards, and application-
specific trust stores. A complete inventory must therefore include both network-facing and
internal cryptographic dependencies.

9       Migration Framework and Comparative Analysis
9.1       Migration Principle
The evidence supports treating PQ TLS as a staged migration architecture. The following
sequence is an analytical synthesis of standards and published evidence rather than a
formally validated algorithm or universal timetable:

    1. Cryptographic inventory. Identify TLS libraries, key-exchange groups, signature
       algorithms, certificates, certificate authorities, trust stores, HSMs, protocols, lifetimes,
       dependencies, and owners.

    2. Identify HNDL-sensitive information. Prioritize information whose confiden- tiality
       must survive for years or decades because present-day collection creates future
       decryption risk [Nat26].

    3. Assess TLS dependencies. Include clients, servers, proxies, middleboxes, load bal-
       ancers, service meshes, certificate-management systems, HSMs, and embedded cryp-
       tographic dependencies.

    4. Deploy and test hybrid key establishment. Where interoperability and im- plemen-
       tation support permit, evaluate hybrid ECDHE-ML-KEM using negotiation success,
       handshake size, CPU use, latency, and fallback behavior.

9.3      Comparison with Previous Surveys
Alnahawi et al. provided a broad 2024 survey of post-quantum TLS, including classifi-
cation and extensive performance evaluation [AMOW24]. Its value lies in establishing
a comprehensive view of candidate PQ TLS mechanisms and their performance at that
stage of the field. The present SoK differs primarily in analytical decomposition. Rather
than treating PQ TLS primarily as a collection of candidate key-exchange mechanisms,
it systematizes the migration as a combination of key establishment, authentication,
PSK/resumption, KeyUpdate, PKI, interoperability, deployment, and crypto-agility. This
distinction is motivated by standards evolution since 2024 rather than by publication
date alone. Broader surveys of quantum-safe network protocols provide useful context
across TLS, IPsec, SSH, PGP, and related systems [BCH24], while PQC migration reviews
identify organizational challenges such as implementation effort, security uncertainty, and
migration complexity [NHG+ 24]. The present work specializes those concerns to TLS and
its certificate ecosystem. The resulting distinction is: PQC TLS ̸= one cryptographic
replacement. Instead:
    Key establishment + authentication + resumption + key evolution + PKI + deployment
+ crypto-agility. This decomposition prevents two recurring analytical errors: treating
KeyUpdate as fresh PQ establishment and assuming that replacing a KEM automatically
produces quantum-resistant authentication.

10     Research Gaps and Discussion
10.1     PQ Authentication and PKI
The literature and standards activity indicate that key-establishment migration is pro-
gressing faster than universal PQ authentication deployment. ML-DSA and SLH-DSA are
standardized algorithms, but deployment requires TLS signature integration, X.509 support,
CA support, HSM support, client validation, and trust-store migration. The research
need is therefore not another signature algorithm alone. It is end-to- end evaluation of
certificate issuance, validation, chaining, trust-anchor migration, HSM integration, and
client interoperability.



10.2     Hybrid Interoperability
Hybrid TLS implementations can differ in supported groups, draft revisions, wire formats,
certificate handling, and fallback behavior. Interoperability research should therefore move
from isolated primitive tests toward standardized cross-implementation test matrices. A
useful test suite should include initial key exchange, authentication, resumption, 0-RTT,
HelloRetryRequest, certificate chains, KeyUpdate, error handling, downgrade scenarios,
and middlebox behavior.

10.3     Performance and Benchmark Standardization
Published studies do not establish one universal PQ TLS performance penalty. CPU-
oriented measurements can show modest computational overhead while network-level
experiments reveal significant latency effects from larger handshake messages. The apparent
disagreement is largely explained by measurement scope. Future bench- mark suites should
report hardware, operating system, TLS implementation, cryptographic library, compiler,
security level, network RTT, packet loss, certificate chain, resumption rate, and concurrency.
Without this metadata, benchmark values are difficult to compare.

10.4     Migration Automation and Cryptographic Inventory
Organizations cannot migrate cryptography they cannot identify. Public-key dependencies
may exist in TLS libraries, certificates, CA systems, HSMs, software, firmware, APIs, and
embedded devices. Migration automation should discover TLS versions, key-exchange
groups, signature algorithms, certificates, CA dependencies, HSM dependencies, software
libraries, hard- coded algorithms, and embedded cryptographic components. A useful
inventory should record at least: (system, algorithm, key, certificate, protocol, lifetime,
dependency, owner). This enables risk prioritization according to data lifetime and
migration difficulty.

10.5     Long-Lived Sessions, PSKs, and Post-Compromise Recovery
The interaction among initial hybrid handshakes, resumption PSKs, KeyUpdate, fresh PQ
rekeying, and endpoint compromise remains insufficiently systematized. Research should
distinguish passive compromise, temporary endpoint compromise, persistent compromise,
compromise before and after KeyUpdate, compromise of the original classical handshake,
compromise of a PQ handshake, and compromise of resumption credentials. The par-
ticularly important question is when a long-lived session should perform fresh PQ key
establishment rather than relying on symmetric key evolution.

10.6     HSM and Certificate Infrastructure
HSM migration remains an infrastructure bottleneck. Research should evaluate PQ key
generation, signing, secure backup, rotation, hybrid signing, certificate issuance, and
performance under high CA loads. Certificate-transparency infrastructure also requires
attention because larger PQ certifi- cates may increase storage, submission bandwidth,
proof- size, and monitoring requirements.

10.7     What the Literature Agrees On
The evidence consistently supports several conclusions: classical public-key mechanisms
create a long-term quantum migration problem; HNDL makes migration relevant before
a cryptographically relevant quantum computer exists [Nat26]; ML-KEM is standardized
by NIST [Nat24b]; hybrid key establishment is standardized for specific TLS 1.3 groups
in RFC 10024 [KKWS26]; authentication and key establishment are separate migration
problems; and cryptographic inventory and crypto-agility are operational prerequisites.

10.8     Where Evidence Differs
The most visible differences concern performance. Some studies report relatively small
computational overheads, whereas network-oriented evaluations show that larger hand-
shake messages can increase latency under specific conditions [rus24, SWH+ 23, M+ 26].
These observations are not necessarily contradictory. A primitive benchmark measures

cryptographic computation, whereas a deployment benchmark measures complete protocol
behavior over a network. Both can be correct. A similar distinction applies to deployment
maturity. The existence of an implementa- tion demonstrates technical feasibility but does
not establish universal interoperability, standardized wire behavior, client support, HSM
support, or production readiness.

10.9     What Is Mature and What Is Evolving
TLS 1.3, classical ECDHE, X.509/PKIX, and the NIST PQ algorithms are comparatively
mature components. The exact TLS integration of PQ algorithms, PQ authentication,
hybrid certificate formats, widespread PQ trust-anchor deployment, HSM support, and
cross-vendor interoperability remain more fluid; several relevant IETF documents remain
Internet-Drafts or are Informational RFCs. This distinction is critical to responsible
migration planning. An
    organization can begin inventory and hybrid experimentation even while avoiding
claims that every component of the eventual PQ ecosystem is finalized.

10.10      Integrated Findings
Across the evidence, the strongest conclusions are those that survive changes in imple-
mentation and standards version. Finding 1 — Migration is multidimensional. Key
establishment, authentication, resumption, traffic-key evolution, PKI, and deployment
are related components of one TLS architecture but are not substitutes for one another.
Finding 2 — Fresh entropy is the decisive distinction for re-establishment. KeyUpdate and
resumption can change connection state without introducing a new PQ foundation. A fresh
PQ-capable exchange is analytically different because new KEM-derived entropy enters
the key schedule. Finding 3 — Hybridization is transitional rather than terminal. Hybrid
ECDHE-ML-KEM provides a rationale for retaining a mature classical component while
adding a PQ component. It should therefore be evaluated as a migration architecture, not
as proof that all uncertainty has disappeared. Finding 4 — Authentication migration is an
ecosystem problem. The cryptographic algorithm, TLS signature negotiation, certificate
representation, CA issuance, HSM, trust anchor, and verifier must all align. A deploy-
ment can be cryptographically capable but operationally unable to validate the resulting
certificate chain. Finding 5 — Performance is a systems property. Primitive cost, TLS
handshake cost, network cost, and certificate-chain cost answer different questions. A single
percentage overhead is therefore not a meaningful universal characterization. Finding 6
— Inventory and crypto-agility are prerequisites. An organization cannot systematically
migrate cryptography that it cannot identify, and it cannot stage replacement safely if
cryptographic mechanisms are hard-coded across applications and infrastructure. Finding
7 — Evidence maturity must be explicit. Finalized standards, active drafts, implementa-
tions, experiments, and production deployment are different evidence classes. Conflating
them creates misleading maturity claims. These findings are the basis for the migration
framework rather than consequences of a particular implementation benchmark.


11      Limitations
This SoK has several limitations. First, the standards landscape is rapidly evolving.
Internet- Drafts discussed here may become RFCs, change substantially, or be replaced
after manuscript preparation. Second, the literature has publication bias toward successful
prototypes and positive benchmark results. Failed migrations and negative interoperability
results are less visible. Third, performance comparisons are heterogeneous. Differences in
hardware, software,

    network conditions, certificate chains, and connection patterns limit direct comparison
of published measurements. Fourth, implementation availability does not establish universal
interoperability. Fifth, the paper does not claim an exhaustive database-indexed systematic
review with a verified numerical corpus. It instead provides a reproducible source-selection
and classification methodology centered on authoritative standards and primary technical
evidence. Sixth, PQ certificate migration remains sufficiently immature that universal
claims about browser, operating-system, HSM, CA, and trust-store compatibility should
be treated cautiously. Seventh, the analysis of PSKs and KeyUpdate is architectural and
standards-based rather than the result of a new formal security proof. Finally, no new
benchmarks, packet captures, interoperability experiments, simula- tions, datasets, or
implementation measurements were conducted for this manuscript. Quantitative evidence
is secondary evidence from cited sources.


12     Conclusion
Post-quantum TLS migration is not a single algorithm-replacement problem. TLS com-
bines key establishment, authentication, resumption, traffic-key evolution, and certificate
infrastructure, and each function has a different security objective and deployment depen-
dency. The central contribution of this SoK is to make those dependencies explicit and to
analyze migration through security lineage rather than through algorithm names alone.
The systematization shows why confidentiality and authentication must be coordinated
but separately evaluated. Hybrid ECDHE-ML-KEM is a strong transitional architecture for
confidentiality migration when the relevant TLS integration and implementation support
are available, because the hybrid construction is designed so that the resulting keying
material can remain secure if one component remains secure. This conclusion does not
imply that the hybrid mechanism is a finalized universal deployment standard, nor does
it eliminate the need for interoperability, downgrade, and implementation analysis. The
analysis of PSKs, resumption, and KeyUpdate produces a second central result. These
mechanisms are not interchangeable forms of rekeying. PSKs can authenticate and can par-
ticipate in key establishment; their security depends on provenance, entropy, provisioning,
and lifecycle. Resumption creates new connection state that remains related to an earlier
handshake. KeyUpdate derives new traffic secrets from an existing traffic-secret generation
and does not introduce an independent PQ secret. Fresh PQ key establishment is therefore
complementary to KeyUpdate rather than replaceable by it. Authentication migration
presents a separate systems problem. ML-DSA and SLH-DSA are finalized NIST signa-
ture standards, and ML-DSA and SLH-DSA now have standardized X.509/PKIX algorithm
identifiers. Nevertheless, deployment requires coordinated support across TLS signature
negotiation, certificate issuance and validation, CA infrastructure, HSMs, trust anchors,
clients, operating systems, and application-specific trust stores. Algorithm standardization
therefore marks an enabling milestone, not the completion of migration. The resulting
migration architecture is:
    Inventory → HNDL assessment → hybrid/PQ key establishment → interoperability
testing → staged PQ authentication → PKI and trust-anchor migration → controlled
retirement of classical-only mechanisms. This sequence is not a universal timetable. The
ordering should be adapted to confidentiality lifetime, endpoint control, compliance re-
quirements, protocol support, interoperability observations, implementation maturity, and
operational constraints. Long-lived sessions require an additional policy decision: when
the threat model or confidentiality lifetime warrants a fresh PQ-capable exchange rather
than continued symmetric key evolution. Finally, the SoK identifies a broader opera-
tional principle. Post-quantum readiness is not established when a single cryptographic
primitive becomes available. It is established when the surrounding system can discover
its cryptographic dependencies, negotiate compatible mechanisms, authenticate peers,

manage certificates and keys, interoperate across the actual communication path, measure
the resulting costs, and replace mechanisms without redesigning the entire application.
Cryptographic inventory and crypto-agility are therefore not peripheral migration practices;
they are enabling conditions for sustained security as the standards and implementation
ecosystem continues to evolve.
